node.label: Walter Johnson
node.date_label: Soul by Soul (1999) · “On Agency” (2003) · River of Dark Dreams: Slavery and Empire in the Cotton Kingdom (2013)
node.description: A historian of American slavery who interrogates the categories historians use to describe enslaved people. “On Agency” argues that treating the discovery of agency as the culmination of slavery history can reproduce liberal assumptions and obstruct attention to historically specific human experience.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Soul by Soul (1999); “On Agency” (2003); River of Dark Dreams: Slavery and Empire in the Cotton Kingdom (2013).

incident_edges.relationship: Questions histories that make recovering agency the endpoint of interpreting slavery.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Read article, especially opening problem and closing methodological discussion; criticism is of an analytic habit rather than of enslaved action itself.

incident_edges.relationship: Calls for historically specific accounts of enslaved humanity, action and collective life beyond the agency/resistance formula.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Read article’s distinction between humanity and agency, with its caution about liberal notions of autonomous selfhood. This is a methodological contribution to slavery history, not a claim every case has been independently verified.

incident_edges.relationship: Johnson challenges Genovese’s paternalism/hegemony account and a sharp individual/collective resistance opposition (2001), then specifies objections about revolutionary aspiration, coercive force and resistance in “On Agency” (2003), without saying Genovese ignored enslaved agency.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Two separately dated primary interventions consolidated as one relationship. 2001 scholarly rereading: Johnson challenges Genovese’s paternalism/hegemony account and the sharp opposition between individual resistance and collective revolt, while affirming the book’s lasting value (2001). Complete scholarly rereading. Johnson argues for coerced rule and a continuum of resistance; he explicitly rejects the simplistic charge that Genovese denied enslaved people agency. Original historical examples and Roll, Jordan, Roll remain uncollated. Reading extent: Fresh complete review read through the final day-to-day resistance paragraph. Distinguishes Genovese’s hegemony argument from denying enslaved agency; criticizes paternalism, coerced rule and a strict individual/collective resistance opposition while affirming the book’s value. The original book and historical examples are not independently audited. 2003 “On Agency”: Johnson rejects three premises of Genovese’s resistance/hegemony account while rejecting the claim that Roll, Jordan, Roll simply ignores enslaved agency (2003). The named p. 117 criticism concerns revolutionary aspiration, culture versus coercive force, and the individual/collective distinction. It is not a denial that Genovese discussed resistance. Reading extent: Fresh primary pp113–114,117 and122–123 read; Genovese’s books were not newly read. These are not a single publication or a second independent edge. The original Genovese book and underlying historical examples are not independently collated.

incident_edges.relationship: Johnson explicitly uses Marx’s Eighteenth Brumaire formulation as an alternative starting point for rethinking agency (2003).
incident_edges.evidence_note: The opening counterposes Marx’s constrained history-making formulation to Gutman’s Sartre-derived injunction; no universal Marxist lineage is inferred.

named_group_routes.relationship: Households placed on the urban lot: linked parish, census and tax records for nineteenth-century Montreal, mapped with GIS at McGill in the 1990s and built from 2000 into the collective MAP geodatabase
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, her own words. 'Le peuplement de Montréal' (Atlas historique du Québec, 1997; read in full) works from 'l’exemple local pour ensuite faire ressortir la vue d’ensemble et saisir ainsi, dans une démarche exploratoire, les processus par lesquels la cité se construit' (p. 81). Its samples are built from records, and differ by population: the Catholic baptismal cohort of 1859, whose parents were traced through the Drouin index and the Notre-Dame registers (n. 4); for the Protestant population only, a micro-sample of ten surnames ('Pour la population protestante, notre microéchantillon s’appuie sur dix patronymes', p. 85), distinct from the twelve-surname sampling that the publisher's description gives for the later book with Thornton (2011, unread here); a 'Montréal « miniaturisé »' of 370 household heads in 1900, and building tradesmen from the 'rôle d’évaluation' plotted in half-kilometre rings 'à la manière d’une reconstitution cinématographique' (p. 89). Note 1 credits the demographic analysis to Patricia Thornton and the mapping 'sur ATLAS GIS' to Ben Johnson and Ingrid Olson, with the McGill GIS laboratory. Earlier work is known only at title level ('Occupations and Residential Spaces', Historical Methods, 1989) or from an abstract (with Gilliland, Urban History Review, 1998: 'From small samples of the Montreal population over the years 1861-1901'). After 2000, her own words. In 2004 she describes the method and its limits: cross-referencing the 1842 census, the 1848 directory and the 1848 taxroll 'in an iterative process of matching surnames, first names, streets of residence, and occupations'; of 5,192 taxroll entries '75 per cent can be matched to the directory, 45 per cent to the census 5 years earlier, and 41 per cent to both sources' (Labour/Le Travail 53, pp. 173–74). In the same note Robert Sweeny 'has created from the Cane map an electronic framework' (p. 165, note). With Dufaux (2014): MAP is 'a collective project in which dozens of people have invested their skills'; 'The spatial links place the household on the cadastral lot – 7,000 lots in the 1850s, 30,000 in 1900' (p. 155); 'A dozen Montreal scholars and a dozen graduate students initiated the project in 2000' (p. 176 n. 1). From abstracts: the 2010 and 2011 papers with Gilliland (and Gauvreau) locate '17,000 individual households' in 1881 and re-aggregate lots into 'districts with identical boundaries for both years', 'overcoming the major methodological problems hindering previous comparative analyses'. Reception (later readings, labelled). Bonnell and Fortin (2014, p. xii): 'Since the 1990s, only a small number of historical geographers and historians have used GIS technology' in Canada; 'Notable projects include Montréal, l’avenir du passé, a comprehensive HGIS database of Montreal led by McGill geographer Sherry Olson and Memorial University historian Robert Sweeny'; 'Olson, Sweeny, and Gilliland’s work has captured the interest of a new generation of graduate students and new scholars' (p. xiii). Lutz, Dunae, Gilliland, Lafreniere and Harvey (2014, p. 11): 'we are following the lead of Sherry Olson, whose pioneering work on nineteenth-century Montreal is a model of spatial history'; their n. 31 lists her 'foundational studies'. That chapter is not independent: Gilliland was her MAP collaborator. Contested: Sweeny, MAP's co-director (Digital Studies, 2009), argues that 'The ontology of geographic information systems is antithetical to historical understanding', that a GIS ensures 'the illusion of accuracy', and that 'an historical GIS works because it is a-historical'. This is a critique of the instrument from inside the project, not of Olson. Not a founding: the editors give the US and British national repositories as 'some of the most important work in the field' (p. xi), and the strand's Gregory and Southall (1998) is a separate, aggregate-boundary tradition. 'Pioneering' is the Victoria team's word, not this entry's.

Abstract: 'Montréal l'avenir du passé (MAP) was established in 2000 to create an historical GIS research infrastructure for 19th and 20th century Montréal. It consists of six highly detailed digitized historical maps representing all buildings in the city for 1825, 1846, 1880, 1912, 1949 and 2000. The first three and last have been geo-referenced and they have been "peopled" by linking at the street-scape (1846) or lot level (1880 & 2000) census returns, tax records, city directories and a wide variety of non-routinely generated sources.'

verification.note: The preface reading recorded below (2026-10-14) was made in a university course-site transcription, a route excluded by the provenance rule of 2026-10-19; the link was replaced on 2026-10-22 (revision 1.152) by the publisher's page for the Penguin Modern Classics edition (ISBN 9780141976952, paperback 3 October 2013; page checked 2026-10-22; it does not reproduce the preface). New text in revision 1.152 attributes the preface's positions through named readers (Eley and Nield 2000 and 2007; Cooper 2000) and makes no new direct quotation; the earlier reading and the quotations it supports on edge_924 are preserved here as recorded. Earlier record: Complete four-page transcription read, including acknowledgments: class as a historical relationship, conditioned experience and culturally formed consciousness, criticism of reification and static social roles, failed causes, English scope and Dorothy’s ideas/notebooks. Smelser and Dahrendorf are named targets; Hill, Briggs and Saville read drafts. Transcription has errors and is not collated with the printed edition. This is the primary preface, not a full-book reading or validation of its historical claims. Addendum 2026-10-14: Re-read in full for the 1.134 extra edge (ep_thompson → karl). Transcription pp. 1–2: 'There is today an ever-present temptation to suppose that class is a thing. This was not Marx's meaning, in his own historical writing, yet the error vitiates much latter-day "Marxist" writing'; the class-consciousness '"it" ought to have'; 'a cultural superstructure, through which this recognition dawns in inefficient ways'; 'a similar error is committed daily on the other side of the ideological divide' (Smelser, Dahrendorf); 'If we remember that class is a relationship and not a thing, we can not think in this way.' Transcription p. 3: the 'enormous condescension of posterity' passage answers Fabian, empirical economic-history and 'Pilgrim's Progress' orthodoxies. Rogers (2021, n. 1) places the class-consciousness passage at pp. 9–10 of the 1968 Penguin edition; printed pages were not checked.
